"'''Without You'''" is a song written by [[Pete Ham]] and [[Tom Evans (musician)|Tom Evans]] of [[Music of Wales|Welsh]] rock group [[Badfinger]], and first released on their 1970 album ''[[No Dice]]''. The [[power ballad]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.loudersound.com/features/the-40-greatest-power-ballads-playlist|title=The 40 Greatest Power Ballads Playlist|website=Classic Rock Magazine|date=14 February 2015|access-date=24 April 2021|archive-date=29 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529112001/https://www.loudersound.com/features/the-40-greatest-power-ballads-playlist|url-status=live}}</ref> has been recorded by over 180 artists,<ref>According to the [[American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers|ASCAP]]</ref> and versions released as singles by [[Harry Nilsson]] (1971) and [[Mariah Carey]] (1994) became international number one hits. The Nilsson version was included in 2021's [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|''Rolling Stone''{{'}}s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|date=2021-09-15|title=The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-11-08|magazine=Rolling Stone|language=en-US|archive-date=22 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122221242/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/}}</ref> [[Paul McCartney]] once described it as "the killer song of all time".<ref name="VH1 Behind The Music">Paul McCartney [http://www.vh1.com/shows/dyn/behind_the_music/51359/episode.jhtml VH1 Behind The Music] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081112092741/http://www.vh1.com/shows/dyn/behind_the_music/51359/episode.jhtml |date=12 November 2008 }}, Retrieved 10 June 2009</ref>

In 1972, Ham and Evans received the British Academy's [[Ivor Novello Award]] for [[Ivor Novello Award for Best Song Musically and Lyrically|Best Song Musically and Lyrically]].<ref>Lister, David, ''Pop ballads bite back in lyrical fashion'', [[The Independent]], 28 May 1994</ref>

sections.heading: Badfinger original
sections.wikitext:
First recorded by the rock group [[Badfinger]], the song was composed by two of its members. [[Pete Ham]] wrote a song originally titled "If It's Love", but it had lacked a strong chorus. At the time of writing, the band shared residence with the [[Mojos]] at [[7 Park Avenue]] in [[Golders Green]]. One evening, in the midst of the parties, songwriting, touring, in Golders Green, Ham and his girlfriend Beverly Tucker were about to go out for the evening. But just as they were leaving Tom Evans said he had an idea for a song – Ham said, "Not tonight, I've promised Bev." But she thought he would be wondering if he had done the right thing later, if he went out. She told him, "Go into the studio, I'm fine about it..."{{nbsp}} He replied, "Your mouth is smiling, but your eyes are sad." The song Ham wrote that night was called "If it's Love" and has the verse "Well I can't forget tomorrow, when I think of all my sorrow, I had you there but then I let you go, and now it's only fair that I should let you know{{nbsp}}... if it's love". But Ham wasn't happy with the chorus.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00y8x91|title=BBC Radio 2 – Song Stories, Without You|publisher=BBC|date=9 February 2011|access-date=27 March 2014|archive-date=1 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001024358/http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00y8x91|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=stereo>{{cite web|title=The Number Ones: Nilsson's "Without You"|author=Breihan, Tom|date=20 February 2019|access-date=2023-05-04|publisher=Stereogum|url=https://www.stereogum.com/2032633/the-number-ones-nilssons-without-you/columns/the-number-ones/}}</ref>

Evans' relationship with his future wife Marianne influenced his lyrics:
{{blockquote|One evening he [Evans] went to her [Marianne's] friend Karen and told Karen, "She's left me. I need her back. I can't live without her." He flew to [[Bonn]] to find her – he wrote a song called "I Can't Live". Its chorus included "I can't live, if living is without you, I can't live, I can't give any more." And so the merging of the two songs,<ref name="BadfingerWithoutYouBBC">{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/music/sites/welsh-love-songs/pages/badfinger-without-you.shtml|title=Badfinger – Without You|publisher=[[BBC Wales]]|access-date=2 May 2011|archive-date=19 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151019131808/http://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/music/sites/welsh-love-songs/pages/badfinger-without-you.shtml|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=stereo/> Ham and Evans created the hit [with] Ham's verse, "warm, sweet, sentimental" and Evans' chorus, "intense, dramatic, heartbreaking."<ref>Song Stories, Radio 2, 9 February 2011</ref>}}
Both Ham and Evans said they did not consider the song to have much potential at the time Badfinger recorded it, and the track was slotted to close the first side of their 1970 album ''No Dice''. Badfinger's recording of the song, which is more brusque than its successors' versions, was not released as a single in Europe or North America.

''Stereogum'' reviewer Tom Breihan said of Badfinger's version that it "is strummy and direct, but it also sounds like a blueprint, not a final version. They could’ve turned it into a showstopping ballad, but they didn’t."<ref name=stereo/>

''Ultimate Classic Rock'' critic Michael Gallucci rated it as Badfinger's 4th-best song, calling it a "quiet gem" that "hits all the right emotional notes."<ref>{{cite web|title=Top 10 Badfinger Songs|author=Gallucci, Michael|publisher=Ultimate Classic Rock|access-date=2023-04-09|date=26 April 2013|url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/badfinger-songs/}}</ref> ''Classic Rock'' critic Rob Hughes rated it Badfinger's 6th-best song, saying it is "less saccharine and more understated [than the Nilsson and Carey versions], delivered with a genuine sense of anguish."<ref name=louder>{{cite web|title=The top 10 best Badfinger songs|author=Hughes, Rob|publisher=Louder Sound|work=Classic Rock|access-date=2023-04-06|date=26 June 2016|url=https://www.loudersound.com/features/the-top-10-best-badfinger-songs}}</ref> [[Paul McCartney]] called it "the killer song of all time."<ref name=louder/>

The two writers of the song, Ham and Evans, later died by suicide due to legal and financial issues.  In Evans' case, it was a dispute over songwriting royalties for "Without You" that precipitated his action. Songwriting royalties had become the subject of constant legal wrangling for Evans, and in 1983, following an acrimonious argument with his bandmate [[Joey Molland]] over the royalties for the song, Evans hanged himself.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/badfinger-last-act-in-a-rock-n-roll-tragedy-8590656.html|title=Badfinger: last act in a rock'n'roll tragedy|first=Nick|last=Clark|date=26 April 2013|work=The Independent|access-date=29 November 2021|archive-date=12 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112004938/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/badfinger-last-act-in-a-rock-n-roll-tragedy-8590656.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3rmJCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA20|title=Suicide in the Entertainment Industry: An Encyclopedia of 840 Twentieth Cases|first=David K.|last=Frasier|date=11 September 2015|page=20|isbn=978-1-4766-0807-5|publisher=McFarland}}</ref>

sections.heading: Background and history
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Harry Nilsson (1973).png|thumb|upright|Harry Nilsson ''(pictured in 1972)'' covered Badfinger's song "Without You".]]
[[Harry Nilsson]], at the time best known for his hit "[[Everybody's Talkin']]" and for composing "[[One (Harry Nilsson song)|One]]", recorded by [[Three Dog Night]], heard Badfinger's recording of "Without You" at a party,{{sfn|Matovina|2000|p=152}} and mistook it for a [[The Beatles|Beatles]] song.<ref name=stereo/> 

After realising it was not, he decided to [[cover version|cover]] the song for his 1971 album ''[[Nilsson Schmilsson]]''.  According to Breihan, "He wanted his version of the song to be a stark, heavy solo-piano thing, but [producer Richard] Perry convinced him to turn it into a grand, crashing, theatrical monster-ballad, complete with orchestra."<ref name=stereo/> [[Gary Wright]], who worked with Badfinger on George Harrison's projects, played the piano. Also featured are [[Klaus Voormann]] (bass), [[Jim Keltner]] (drums) and John Uribe (acoustic guitar). The string and horn arrangements are by [[Paul Buckmaster]].

thumb|upright|Harry Nilsson (pictured in 1972) covered Badfinger's song "Without You".
Harry Nilsson, at the time best known for his hit "Everybody's Talkin'" and for composing "One", recorded by Three Dog Night, heard Badfinger's recording of "Without You" at a party,{{sfn|Matovina|2000|p=152}} and mistook it for a Beatles song. 

After realising it was not, he decided to cover the song for his 1971 album Nilsson Schmilsson.  According to Breihan, "He wanted his version of the song to be a stark, heavy solo-piano thing, but [producer Richard] Perry convinced him to turn it into a grand, crashing, theatrical monster-ballad, complete with orchestra." Gary Wright, who worked with Badfinger on George Harrison's projects, played the piano. Also featured are Klaus Voormann (bass), Jim Keltner (drums) and John Uribe (acoustic guitar). The string and horn arrangements are by Paul Buckmaster.

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext:
The single was released by [[RCA Corporation|RCA]] in the autumn of 1971, and it first charted on radio stations across the US in early December. "Without You" debuted at number 99 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] on 18 December 1971, and on its tenth week, in the chart dated 19 February 1972, started its four-week run at number one, as his only song to peak at that position. ''Billboard'' ranked it as the number-four single of 1972. The record topped ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Hot Adult Contemporary Tracks|Easy Listening chart]] for five weeks.

The record spent five weeks at number one on the [[UK singles chart]], beginning on 11 March, eventually selling almost 800,000 copies.<ref>Dafydd Rees and Luke Crampton, Rock Stars Encyclopedia (New York: DK Publishing, 1999), 714.</ref> It went to number one in several other countries, including Australia (for five weeks), Ireland (two weeks) and New Zealand (two weeks).

The single was re-released in 1976 where it went back to [[List of number-one singles of 1976 (Ireland)|number one in Ireland]] for two weeks and peaked at #22 in the UK.<ref>{{Cite web|date=1969-09-27|title=NILSSON|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/13778/nilsson/|access-date=2024-11-26|publisher=Official Charts Company|language=en}}</ref>

The single was released by RCA in the autumn of 1971, and it first charted on radio stations across the US in early December. "Without You" debuted at number 99 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 18 December 1971, and on its tenth week, in the chart dated 19 February 1972, started its four-week run at number one, as his only song to peak at that position. Billboard ranked it as the number-four single of 1972. The record topped Billboard{{'}}s Easy Listening chart for five weeks.

The record spent five weeks at number one on the UK singles chart, beginning on 11 March, eventually selling almost 800,000 copies. It went to number one in several other countries, including Australia (for five weeks), Ireland (two weeks) and New Zealand (two weeks).

The single was re-released in 1976 where it went back to number one in Ireland for two weeks and peaked at #22 in the UK.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' said it was "by far [Nilsson's] most commercial driving rock ballad in some time."<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|access-date=2023-04-09|date=4 December 1971|title=Spotlight Singles|page=52|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/70s/1971/Billboard%201971-12-04.pdf}}</ref> ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' said of the single "Couple a winning Badfinger tune with Gary Wright's piano and Nilsson's wideranging voice, and you've got Harry's biggest hit since '[[Everybody's Talkin']].'"<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Cashbox|access-date=2023-04-09|date=4 December 1971|page=14|title=Cashbox Singles Reviews|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/70s/1971/Cash-Box-1971-12-04.pdf}}</ref> ''[[Record World]]'' said that "Nilsson's brilliant rendition of this Badfinger song has more than enough of the stuff of which hits are made."<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Picks of the Week|magazine=Record World|date=4 December 1971|page=1|access-date=2023-04-09|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/71/RW-1971-12-04.pdf}}</ref> Breihan described the song as "going-for-it schmaltz," compared with Badfinger's "vaguely embarrassed schmaltz", but basically considered it a "big and silly and down-the-middle breakup ballad."<ref name=stereo/> 

The single, Grammy-nominated for [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]], was produced by [[Richard Perry]], who later explained, "It was a different record for its time. It was a big ballad with a heavy backbeat, and although many artists have cut songs like it since, no one was doing it then."<ref name="super">{{cite web|url=http://www.superseventies.com/1972_3singles.html|title="Without You" – Nilsson|publisher=Superseventies.com|date=19 February 1972|access-date=27 March 2014|archive-date=1 December 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101201094709/http://www.superseventies.com/1972_3singles.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The recording has since been considered by some to be one of the first [[Sentimental ballad|power ballads]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=published |first=Neil Crossley |date=2024-11-09 |title=“He wanted his version of the song to be a stark, heavy solo-piano thing, but they convinced him to turn it into a grand, crashing, theatrical monster-ballad, complete with orchestra”: The story of Nilsson's Without You |url=https://www.musicradar.com/artists/singers-songwriters/he-wanted-his-version-of-the-song-to-be-a-stark-heavy-solo-piano-thing-but-they-convinced-him-to-turn-it-into-a-grand-crashing-theatrical-monster-ballad-complete-with-orchestra-the-story-of-nilssons-without-you |access-date=2026-04-09 |website=MusicRadar |language=en}}</ref> In 1973, the single won Nilsson the [[Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance|Grammy award for Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male]].{{sfn|Matovina|2000|p=209}}  While Nilsson rarely gave live concerts, he did perform the song with [[Ringo Starr]] and his [[Ringo Starr & His All-Starr Band|All-Starr Band]] at Caesar's Palace in [[Las Vegas Valley|Las Vegas]] in September 1992.<ref>Chip Madinger and Mark Easter, Eight Arms To Hold You: The Solo Beatles Compendium (Chesterfield, MO: 44.1 Productions, 2000), 543.</ref>

In 1972 Evans said of finding out that Nilsson had recorded the song as a single:{{quote|We were in our studios in London. We'd gone through one of those periods where things weren't going too well. This guy came in and said "Are you Badfinger? I'm Harry Nilsson. I've got this song to play for you." It was his version of "Without You." He said he was going to use it as a single. We're thinking about other songs we can lay on him. No one had recorded any of our songs until then. It had been our ambition to write songs other people would record. It's one of the most exciting things that has happened.<ref>{{cite news|via=Newspapers.com|access-date=2023-04-07|newspaper=The Daily Register|author=Campbell, Mary|title=Badfinger Quartet Thrilled by Gold Record|date=21 April 1972|page=5|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/122455890/the-daily-register/}}</ref>}}

In 2021, this version was ranked 496th on [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|''Rolling Stone''{{'}}s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Without You ranked #496 on Rolling Stone 500 Greatest Songs List|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/harry-nilsson-without-you-1224841/|url-status=live|access-date=24 September 2021|magazine=Rolling Stone|archive-date=16 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210916172706/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/harry-nilsson-without-you-1224841/}}</ref> [[Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark|OMD]] frontman [[Andy McCluskey]] named Nilsson's interpretation as the song that makes him cry, adding, "His voice is so plaintive, so broken, so tearful, it's stunning."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/features/music-interviews/omd-andy-mccluskey-orchestral-manouevres-in-the-dark-3498101|title=Soundtrack of My Life: OMD's Andy McCluskey|last=Beaumont|first=Mark|author-link=Mark Beaumont (journalist)|date=15 September 2023|website=[[NME]]|access-date=14 July 2026}}</ref>

sections.heading: ASCAP and Ivor Novello recognition
sections.wikitext:
{{one source|section|date=May 2018}}
On 15 May 1995, at [[ASCAP]]'s twelfth annual Pop Music Awards in Beverly Hills, California, "Without You" was recognised as one of the 50 most-played songs of 1994 (due largely to Mariah Carey's recording). Discrepancies in ASCAP's books, resulting from a lawsuit against the Ham and Evans estates by their former manager, incorrectly attributed the song as being composed not only by Ham and Evans, but also by Badfinger's other bandmembers, Mike Gibbins and Joey Molland, and their former manager, Bill Collins. This designation and a lack of correction by ASCAP prompted the Ham Estate to boycott the ceremony. The song was also nominated for "Song of the Year" in London at the Ivor Novello Awards.<ref name="Without You: The Tragic Story of Badfinger">, page 395, Matovina, Dan. [https://books.google.com/books?id=eAURGSMNfTUC&dq=%22Without+You:+The+Tragic+Story+of+Badfinger%22&pg=PP1 Without You: The Tragic Story of Badfinger] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230115151154/https://books.google.com/books?id=eAURGSMNfTUC&pg=PP1&dq=%22Without+You:+The+Tragic+Story+of+Badfinger%22&sig=jph9Jp_3_JMMBps7_FvJSZkPHrI |date=15 January 2023 }}, Google Books, 2000. Retrieved 17 June 2009</ref>
sections.text:
{{one source|section|date=May 2018}}
On 15 May 1995, at ASCAP's twelfth annual Pop Music Awards in Beverly Hills, California, "Without You" was recognised as one of the 50 most-played songs of 1994 (due largely to Mariah Carey's recording). Discrepancies in ASCAP's books, resulting from a lawsuit against the Ham and Evans estates by their former manager, incorrectly attributed the song as being composed not only by Ham and Evans, but also by Badfinger's other bandmembers, Mike Gibbins and Joey Molland, and their former manager, Bill Collins. This designation and a lack of correction by ASCAP prompted the Ham Estate to boycott the ceremony. The song was also nominated for "Song of the Year" in London at the Ivor Novello Awards.
